prompt: Narrative theory's foundational distinction is between:
options: Story (what happens) and discourse (how it's told)
correctAnswer: Story (what happens) and discourse (how it's told)
explanation: Same story can be told many ways. French structuralists called these histoire and récit; Russian Formalists used fabula and syuzhet. The distinction lets analysis attend separately to events themselves and to techniques by which they're presented.

prompt: Whose 1972 Narrative Discourse, built on close analysis of Proust, became the central work of modern narrative theory?
explanation: Three main axes: tense (order, duration, frequency), mood (focalisation), voice (who narrates). The book's vocabulary — diegesis, focalisation, analepsis, prolepsis — has become standard in narrative theory.

prompt: Plato's Republic Book 3 distinguished diegesis (telling) from _________ (showing).
explanation: Modern narrative typically combines both — narrator's summary alongside dramatised scenes. Genette uses 'diegetic' more broadly: the world of the story. Extradiegetic = outside the story; intradiegetic = inside it.

prompt: What's the strong critical objection to the story-discourse distinction?
options: 'Story' is itself reconstructed by readers from the discourse — there's no story prior to the telling
correctAnswer: 'Story' is itself reconstructed by readers from the discourse — there's no story prior to the telling
explanation: Jonathan Culler and others have argued this. The distinction remains useful as a tool, with awareness of its limits. Most narrative analysis still works within Genette's framework.

prompt: Match each pair of terms used for story/discourse:
explanation: All three pairs name the same fundamental distinction. The distinction lets formal choices become visible — why this point of view, why this temporal arrangement, why begin where it begins.

prompt: What's analepsis?
options: Flashback — discourse going back in time to an earlier event
correctAnswer: Flashback — discourse going back in time to an earlier event
explanation: Prolepsis is the opposite (flashforward): 'Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember...' (García Márquez). Modern fiction routinely deploys complex order.

prompt: In Genette's duration categories, when discourse compresses story ('Three years passed') it's called:
explanation: Other duration types: scene (discourse time matches story time, mostly dialogue), ellipsis (discourse skips story time entirely), pause (discourse continues while story stops — description), stretch (discourse expands story; a second of consciousness across pages).

prompt: Genette's term for telling once what happened several times ('Every Sunday she went to mass') is _________.
explanation: Frequency types: singulative (telling once what happened once, standard), repetitive (telling several times what happened once — multiple narrators on same event, Rashomon), iterative (telling once what happened several times). Proust's iteratives are famous.

prompt: What's the basic discovery of 20th-century narrative about time?
options: Time can be one of the novelist's primary instruments — naïve chronological telling is one option among many
correctAnswer: Time can be one of the novelist's primary instruments — naïve chronological telling is one option among many
explanation: A novel that ends with the protagonist's death and circles back to childhood (Mrs Dalloway's structural logic) builds different meanings than chronological narration would. The reader knows the future while watching the past.

prompt: Match each Genette temporal category to its description:

pairs.right: Relation between story chronology and discourse sequence; analepsis (flashback), prolepsis (flashforward)
Pages per event; scene, summary, ellipsis, pause, stretch
How often discourse tells; singulative, repetitive, iterative

explanation: Anachrony is any departure from chronological order. Some are internal (within main timeframe), some external (reaching outside it). The technical apparatus matters less than the underlying point: temporal play in narrative is one of fiction's main resources.

prompt: Genette separated 'point of view' into which two distinct categories?
explanation: Often these coincide, but a first-person narrator can report what another character saw, or a third-person narrator can present events from inside a particular character's consciousness. The voice/focalisation distinction has been one of the most useful refinements in narrative theory.

prompt: What is 'zero focalisation'?
options: Omniscient narration — the narrator knows everything (all characters' thoughts, things they don't know)
correctAnswer: Omniscient narration — the narrator knows everything (all characters' thoughts, things they don't know)
explanation: 19th-century novels often use this. Internal focalisation: events through one character's perspective. External focalisation: events from outside any character's consciousness, narrator reports actions but doesn't enter minds (Hemingway's later style approaches this).

prompt: The rare second-person novel by Italo Calvino addressed to 'you' is If on a winter's night a _________.
explanation: Second person is rare and difficult to sustain. Bright Lights, Big City and parts of Bolaño are other examples. Most novels use first or third person; the choice has consequences for intimacy, reliability, and what kinds of knowledge the narrator can plausibly possess.

prompt: What's the most flexible technique for representing minds in third-person narrative?
options: Free indirect discourse — narrator's third-person voice inflected by character's thought without quotation marks
correctAnswer: Free indirect discourse — narrator's third-person voice inflected by character's thought without quotation marks
explanation: Pioneered by Austen, perfected by Flaubert, central to Joyce and Woolf. It allows seamless drift between narrator and character — the reader is now inside, now outside, now both. One of the things that distinguishes the modern novel from earlier prose narrative.

prompt: Match each focalisation type to its character:

pairs.right: Omniscient; narrator knows all characters' thoughts
From outside any consciousness; narrator reports actions but doesn't enter minds

explanation: Internal focalisation can be fixed (one character throughout), variable (different characters in different sections), or multiple (same event from multiple perspectives). Each focalisation choice creates different reader experience and constrains plot.

prompt: Which novelist is generally credited with first sustained use of free indirect discourse in English?
explanation: Emma Woodhouse's misperceptions are filtered through her own consciousness, in language hovering between her perspective and the narrator's. The technique is what makes Austen's irony possible — the narrator never says 'Emma was being foolish'; the text shows Emma being foolish in her own voice.

prompt: Which French novelist perfected FID across hundreds of pages in Madame Bovary (1856)?
explanation: Emma's romantic delusions filtered through her own grandiose vocabulary, the narrator's distance audible without ever being stated. He demonstrated that narrative voice could be a continuous interplay rather than a fixed position. French structuralists made him central to their analysis.

prompt: Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) opens in baby talk because the focal character is a(n) _________.
explanation: 'Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow coming down along the road.' The prose evolves with Stephen's consciousness through the book. By chapter five, the language is theological abstraction — because that's where Stephen's mind has gone.

prompt: What does FID let a writer do that other techniques can't?
options: Get inside characters without losing third-person discipline; produce irony at character's expense; shift perspective fluidly; create intimate unreliability
correctAnswer: Get inside characters without losing third-person discipline; produce irony at character's expense; shift perspective fluidly; create intimate unreliability
explanation: FID is now standard equipment for serious fiction. Most contemporary literary novels use it routinely. Younger readers sometimes find it confusing; the convention has to be learned. Once learned, it's invisible.

prompt: Match each level of speech representation to an example:

pairs.right: She thought that she shouldn't be there.
No — she shouldn't be here at all.

explanation: Free indirect uses the third person and past tense of standard narration but the vocabulary, syntax, and emotional register of the character. The reader hears narrator and character at once. Without FID, most of the great fiction of the past two centuries would be impossible.

prompt: Who introduced the term 'unreliable narrator' in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961)?
explanation: Booth's working definition: a narrator is unreliable when their account diverges from the work's implied norms. The reader perceives a gap between what the narrator says and what the implied author seems to mean. The mechanism requires the reader to do interpretive work.

prompt: Humbert Humbert in Lolita (Nabokov, 1955) is most clearly:
options: Morally and aesthetically unreliable — elaborate aesthetic prose disguising paedophilia
correctAnswer: Morally and aesthetically unreliable — elaborate aesthetic prose disguising paedophilia
explanation: Other types of unreliability: factual (lies, misremembers), naive (doesn't fully understand what they report — the child narrator), mental (perception impaired — Faulkner's Benjy in The Sound and the Fury). Often these combine.

prompt: Ishiguro's 1989 novel narrated by an English butler whose professional dignity has cost him his life is The Remains of the _________.
explanation: Stevens's gradual revelation of how much he has missed makes him one of the most subtle unreliable narrators in modern fiction. Other major examples: Charles Kinbote in Pale Fire, Patrick Bateman in American Psycho, Amy Dunne in Gone Girl.

prompt: How is unreliability typically signalled to readers?
options: Internal contradictions, external evidence (other characters' reactions), language choices that betray hidden attitudes, genre conventions
correctAnswer: Internal contradictions, external evidence (other characters' reactions), language choices that betray hidden attitudes, genre conventions
explanation: Skilled writers vary how strongly they signal. Maximally subtle unreliability — where the reader is gradually destabilised — is harder to write than overt unreliability. The reader has to be able to detect unreliability, but not so easily that the technique becomes heavy-handed.

prompt: Match each unreliable narrator to their work:

pairs.right: Pale Fire (Nabokov, 1962); commentator projecting his life onto a poem he didn't write

explanation: Unreliable narration builds intimacy with a perspective the reader rejects, makes the reader active, and dramatises self-deception and partial vision. Most major modernist and postmodernist novels involve some form of unreliability.
